en: Victory to Śrī Śrī Gaura-Gadādhara!
The First Chapter of the Śrī Saṅgīta Sāra Saṃgraha.
The Section on the Gītā.
Salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa!
Having first prostrated before Śrī Govinda for the sake of the happiness of those who know the Gītā:
In brief, I shall here declare this compendium of the essence of music (*saṅgītasārasaṃgraha*).
Now, regarding the origin of music: in ancient times, the Lotus-born One (Brahmā), having extracted the essence of the four Vedas, [composed it].
But this fifth Veda, known as Saṅgīta, was fashioned. To explain why and what was produced from it, he says:
from the Ṛks the Pāṭha arose, and from the Sāmans the Gīta was accomplished.
From the Yajurveda the Abhinayas were born, and the Rasas are recorded as originating from the Atharvaveda.
Regarding the purity of the tradition, Brahmā, Īśa, Tandi, Bharata, Durga, Nārada, and Kohala [are the authorities].

Daśāsya, Vāyu, Ambha, and Udyā are the propagators of music. Furthermore, he states its excellence [by noting that] even those who know various sciences such as the Śruti, Smṛti, and other literary works [praise it].
Those who do not know music are considered two-legged deer.
In the *Saṅgīta-dāmodara*, it is said that he in whose mind there is no joy from delightful music [is likewise such].
That bull among men in the world was indeed deceived by fate.
He states the purpose:
"All acts such as giving, sacrifice, and praise yield the fruits of the three aims of life."
A single consciousness of song bestows the fruit of the four aims of life;
in Dāmodara, it increases supreme bliss, grants desired fruits, and effects subjugation.
It is proclaimed as the supreme seed of liberation that captivates the hearts of all people.
As for what its essential nature is, it is stated in the *Saṅgītapārijāta*:
"The triad of song, instrumental music, and dance is called *saṅgīta*."
Because singing is the primary element here, it is called *saṅgīta*. In the *Śiromaṇi*,
the triad of song, instrumental music, and dance is termed *saṅgīta*.
Some say that both song and instrumental music together constitute *saṅgīta*.
Thus it is proclaimed that [this song] steals away the delusion of animals, humans, gods,
and others. By this song of Hari from the *Dāmodara*, even birds fall into captivity.
Even young serpents come of their own accord and do not cry out;
yet when a child lies upon a swing of *pārijāta* flowers, he remains there crying at times.
Then, having drunk the nectar of the Gītā, he attains the height of joy.
Even that deer, while wandering through the forest grazing on grass, attains its life's end upon hearing the music from a hunter. ||12-13||
An angry serpent, vomiting venom and repeatedly tossing its hood,
attains a state of extreme joy upon hearing the song of a snake-charmer.
This is also stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Whatever poetic compositions there may be, and all songs whatsoever—
these are portions of the high-souled Viṣṇu, who bears the form of sound.
Even therein:

"A human being, being delighted, should perform singing, instrumental music, and dancing for the god, for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu; thus it is proclaimed in the scripture. I do not dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, nor indeed in the hearts of yogins. (16)
"O Nārada, I abide wherever my devotees sing;
hearing the auspicious [glories] of the Discus-wielder... (Bhāgavata 11.2.39).
Singing the names that correspond to the births and deeds celebrated in the world, one should wander without attachment and free from shame. (18)

The names of Viṣṇu, when composed with beautiful melodies and recited by the wise, become equal to the Sāman chants. Now, [the author] states the two-fold nature of musical performance (*saṅgīta*) in the *Saṅgītasāra*:
According to the division into *mārga* and *deśī*, music is twofold:
that which relies on *mārga* is found in heaven, while that which relies on *deśī* delights the earth.
(Pārijāta 20)

Saṅgīta is said to be twofold, distinguished by the categories of *mārga* and *deśī*. Brahmā himself taught the *saṅgīta* known as *mārga* to Bharata. Having studied the *saṅgīta* designated as *mārga* from Brahmā, Bharata... [21]
And he employed [this] before Śambhu along with the Apsarases and Gandharvas.
(22) Thus they say that music is "regional" (deśīya) according to the distinction of regions.
(23) Since song was mentioned first therein and will be described later, and since it is impossible without sound (nāda), he first describes sound. As it has been said:

There is no song without sound, no musical note without sound, and no melody without sound; therefore, the world is of the nature of sound (nādātmaka). There is no knowledge without sound, and no Śiva without sound.
The supreme light is in the form of sound, and Hari himself is in the form of sound.
And there, even Āñjaneya and Sarasvatī do not know the further shore of that ocean of sound.
Even now, out of fear of being submerged, it carries you upon its breast.
He describes the manner of its arising:
"Since this self, desiring to speak, impels the mind..."
It strikes the fire residing within the body, and that [fire] impels the vital air (māruta).
Thus it is said in the *Saṅgītasāra*:
"The syllable *na* is the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), and the syllable *da* is the bearer of oblations (fire)."
Since it arises from those two, it is therefore called *nāda*.
In common usage, however, this *nāda* is declared by the wise to be threefold:
*mandra* situated in the heart, *madhya* in the throat, and *tāra* in the head.
Each subsequent one is indeed double the size of the preceding one in measurement.
According to Kohālīya, however, that sound is considered to be of two kinds: struck (āhata) and unstruck (anāhata).
That wherein both types of conjunction are struck together is proclaimed as the *anāhata* (unstruck).
The sound (*nāda*) arising from space is likewise called *anāhata*. Having drawn forth the *āhata* sound from that which is designated as *anāhata*, [one should practice].
He split that sound into seven forms by means of the notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*.
In reality, however, [as stated] in the *Saṅgītamuktāvalī*:
"Born from ether, fire, and wind, rising upward from the navel..."
That which attains manifestation in the mouth is proclaimed as *nāda*. It is of two kinds: that which arises from living beings and that which does not arise from living beings.
The first is produced by the body; the second is produced by the lute (*vīṇā*). ||32-33||
"And the third is that which arises from bamboo and other materials; it is considered to be of three kinds.

(34) Thus [ends the section on instruments]. Now, regarding song (*gīta*): its definition varies in many ways according to the differing opinions of various masters. Nevertheless, that which is most widely accepted is stated here in the *Saṅgītasāra*:
"Song is that which is pleasing, and it consists of *dhātu*, *mātra*, and *sahita*."
The components of song, such as the *dhātu* (musical structure) and *rāga* (melodic mood), are said to be its "mother.
As stated in the *Saṅgītakaumudī*: "Song is that which is composed of *rāgas*.
However, in the *Gītaprakāśa*, it is said: "Song is a composition consisting of a collection of pleasing notes."

In reality, however, it is stated in the Nāradasaṃhitā that song is defined as being joined with *dhātu* and *mātu*. In that context, the song consisting of sound (*nāda*) is designated as *dhātu*. (36)
Because it possesses qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, that very [Gītā] is indeed a *dhātu* (element);
if there is charm and vigor within its qualities, ornaments, and sentences, it is called *mātuḥ* by those who know it, due to its delighting human beings. (37)

"Consisting of sound (*nādātmaka*) means that sound itself is its essence or nature. Here, by the word "sound," there is the inclusion of the musical notes (*śrutisvara*) produced from sound. As it has been said:

"From sound the *śrutis* are born; from them the notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*; from those the scales (*mūrcchanās*) arise; and from those come the rhythmic cycles (*tāla*), which are born from the *grāmas*. (38)

And therein, the sequence is as follows: sound (nāda), audition (śruti), note (svara), scale (grāma), modulation (mūrcchanā), rhythm (tāla), syllable (varṇa), the notes known as the tonic (graha) and the final (nyāsa), and the musical genre (jāti). //39//
There are the *grahasvara*, the *aṃśasvara*, and the *nyāsasvara*. Among these, *nāda* has been explained.
Now, regarding the *śrutis*:
that *nāda*, struck by the wind of the *syan*, becomes twenty-two *śrutis*.
Twenty-two [channels] extend upward from the navel toward the heart;
as many as they are, so many are proclaimed to be the *śrutis*.
Their progressive height is observed precisely in the lute (*vīṇā*) and similar instruments.
Because their manifestation does not occur when the throat is afflicted by phlegm and other humors;
these four are considered to be the *śrutis* of the fifth [note], Ṣaḍja, and Madhyama.
In the Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata [tunes], there are three [notes]; in Gāndhāra and Niṣāda, there are two.
What are their names? I say: Nāndī, Viśālā, Sumukhī, and Vicitrā; these are remembered as the Ṣaḍjas.
Citrā, Ghanā, and Cālanikā are said to be the three [melodies] in Ṛṣabha.
In Gāndhāra, Sarasā and Mālā [are mentioned]; in Madhyama, Māgadhī, Śivā, and Mātaṅgikā—these four are proclaimed by Matanga.
Bālā, Kalā, and Kalaravā—these three are for the note Pañcama; Śārṅgiṇī and Avyapi are for Dhaivata; and Mātā and Rasāmṛtā are for Niṣāda.
Furthermore, Vijayā and Madhukarī are for Niṣāda. (45)
Thus, twenty-two *śrutis* of the *svaras* have been declared.

Regarding the phrase "of the *svaras*" (*svarāṇām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of a relationship between producer and produced—just as in the expression "the father of sons"—meaning they are the progenitors of the *svaras*. In reality, however, their true nature is impossible to know. As it is said in the *Saṅgītadāmodara*:
"Even Brahmā himself is not capable of describing the *svaras* in the precise location of the *śrutis*."
Just as the path of fish moving in the waters cannot be perceived,
and just as that of birds in the sky [cannot be seen], so too is the Veda (śruti) situated within its own sound (svara).
The Veda is said to be supported by sound (nāda), and its movement is considered to be through the subtle divisions (kalā).
Just as ghee exists within oil, just as fire exists within wood, and just as the *śruti* exists within the *svara*, it is known here through instruction.
However, the knowledge of *śruti* comes from the lute and similar instruments, while the knowledge of *svara* arises from the flute. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore,
those distinctions among these notes belonging to the same *śruti* which arise from their deviation from practical application have not been described here as distinct *śrutijātis*. (50)
Now, as for the musical notes (*svara*):
a note is that which, vibrating in the locus of audition, is pleasing to the heart.
By this, it is stated that the word *svara* possesses both an etymological (*yoga*) and a conventional (*rūḍhi*) meaning.
"Or rather, because they delight the mind of the listener, they are called *svara*s (notes).
By this, their conventional status (*rūḍhatva*) is stated.
He asks: "Which ones are they? and says:
Ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama,
dhaivata, and niṣāda— these seven notes (svaras) are proclaimed here. Ṣa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni— these are their other designations.
These [sounds] are of three kinds, depending upon the states of low (*mandra*), middle (*madhya*), and high (*tāra*).
Indeed, they have three locations: the low tone is produced in the heart;
the middle in the throat; and the high in the head. Each subsequent one is double the frequency of the preceding.

Regarding these, they state their etymological derivation as follows: "Because it is produced from six [places] by touching the throat, chest, palate, tongue, and teeth, it is therefore known as *ṣaḍja*. (55)
Dāmodara, however, says otherwise:
"When the wind is obstructed in the navel, the channels of the heart, the sides, and also the head, the *ṣaḍja* is produced from these six. (56)
When the wind, having risen from the root of the navel, produces a sound like that of a bull as it issues forth effortlessly,
it is known as *ṛṣabha*.
The wind, having emerged from the navel, causes the sense of smell to vibrate within the ear.
That by which one exits with sound is called Gāndhāra.
Madhyama arises from the middle part of the body; it originates from the root of the navel and is deep, yet slightly acute by its very nature. ||58-59||
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and likewise vyāna—
through the combination of these, the fifth sound is produced.
Having gone to the lower part of the navel and reached the bladder, it moves upward once again.
And that which goes to the region of the throat as if running is the *dhaivata* [61].
These six notes beginning with *ṣaḍja* are all captivating here;
because they exclude (*niṣidanti*) [other sounds] in the world, it is therefore called *niṣāda* [62].
In that regard, by means of describing the sounds corresponding to those [notes],
the peacock proclaims the *ṣaḍja*, the *cātaka* bird speaks the *ṛṣabha*,
the goat announces the *gāndhāra*, and the *krauñca* cries out the *madhyama*. (63)
The cuckoo utters the fifth note (pañcama), the frog speaks the sixth (dhaivata), and the elephant bellows the seventh (niṣāda); this is the consensus of Brahmā and others. But Dāmodara says: [64]
The peacock, the bull, the goat, the curlew, the cuckoo, the horse, and the elephant—these are said to be the [seven] notes in order, which are very difficult to master. Thus it is said;
furthermore:

Furthermore, these notes are said to be of four kinds: the *vādī* (the leading note), the *saṃvādī* (the concordant note), the *vivādī* (the discordant note), and the *anuvādī* (the following note). Among them, that which is called the *vādī* is defined as follows:
it is the one that occurs most frequently in musical performances and expresses the determination of the *rāga* and other elements.
A *samaśruti* (consonant interval) is concordant (*saṃvādī*) with the fifth [note], but the *ma* [note] is never [concordant] with it.
Ga and Ni would be dissonant (*vivādinau*) with respect to Ri and Dha, or those two [notes] with respect to Ga and Ni.
In the remaining cases, they would be consonant (*anuvādī*); such is the opinion of Dantila.

The meaning of this is as follows: that note which, being prevalent—that is, abundant—in musical applications (*prayoga*), expresses the determination of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, and having been stated many times, produces the certainty "this is such-and-such a *rāga*," is the *vādī* (leading) note. That note whose sound is similar to the *saṃśruti* of the fifth [note] is the *saṃvādī* (consonant) note. In some cases, *ma*—that is, the *madhyama* note—is not a *saṃvādī*. *Ga* and *ni*—namely, *gāndhāra* and *niṣāda*—are the *vivādins* (dissonants), acting as enemies, of *ri* and *dha*—namely, *ṛṣabha* and *dhaivata*.

Or, in another view, those two—Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata—are the disputants (*vivādinau*) of Gāndhāra and Niṣāda respectively. The remainder—the notes remaining after these—are the concordant notes (*anuvādisvarāḥ*).
Furthermore:
"The *vādī* (the proponent), the *nṛpa* (the king), as well as the *pātra* (the vessel), are the *saṃvādins* (concordant); the *ari* (enemy) is the *vivādī* (disputant)."
The *anuvādī* is the attendant of the king; [it is] the *cerita* of the vessel. (69) The meaning is that the *anuvādī* is the follower of both the *vādin* and the *samvādī*. Now, the villages.
The "village" (grāma) is the subtle state of the notes; its conjunction consists of three types of pitch-classes (sthānakula).
Among them, Ṣaḍja and Madhyama exist on earth, while that which is named Gāndhāra exists indeed in the world of the gods. (70) — Dāmodara.
In this world of humans, there are both the Ṣaḍja and the Madhyama scales;
in the world of the gods (Sūraloka), the Gāndhāra scale certainly prevails.
Furthermore:
A collection of well-arranged notes is considered a *grāma*. Furthermore, in the *Pārijāta*,
three *grāmas* are described as being composed of a multitude of notes.

Endowed with the names Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Gāndhāra, these constitute the basis for the *mūrchanās*. Among them, the Ṣaḍja-grāma is the most excellent in three respects. (73) Now, he describes the *mūrchanās* of the three *grāmas*:
Sa-ri-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni and ma-pa; dha-ni-sa-ri and ga;
ga-ma-pa and dha-ni-sa-ri—these are the scales (grāma) and the melodic modulations (mūrcchanā).
Furthermore: [74]
In this system, exactly seven *mūrcchanās* are proclaimed for each *grāma*;
they are considered to begin on the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh notes respectively.
This is the sequence of their arrangement.

They say that the *mūrcchanās* of the Ṣaḍja-grāma are as follows: from Ṣaḍja ending with Niṣāda; from Dhaivata ending with Pañcama; from Pañcama ending with Madhyama; from Madhyama ending with Gāndhāra; from Gāndhāra ending with Ṛṣabha; and from Ṛṣabha ending with Pañcama. (76)

The illustration of that is as follows: sa ri ga ma pa dha ni ca; ni sa ri ga ma pa dha ca; dha ni sa ri ga ma pa ca; pa dha ni sa ri ga ma ca; ma pa dha ni sa ri ga ca; ga ma pa dha ni sa ri ca; ri ga ma pa dha ni sa ca. These are the *mūrcchanās* of the Ṣaḍjagrāma.
Now, the *mūrcchanās* of the Madhyamagrāma are described:
from Ma to Gā, from Gā to Ṛṣabha, and from Ṛṣabha to Sa (Saptama) is prescribed.
Ending with *sān*, *nerdh*, *devatān*, *dhātpān*, and *pāccamān*—this is the *ahāraṇa*:

*ma pa dha ni sa ri ga ca*; *ga ma pa dha ni sa ri ca*; *ri ga ma pa dha ni sa ca*; *sa ri ga ma pa dha ni ca*; *ni sa ri ga ma pa dha ca*; *dha ni sa ri ga ma pa ca*; *pa dha ni sa ri ga ma ca*. These are the *mūrcchanās* of the Madhyama-grāma.
Where the syllable *ga* occurs at the beginning, those are the *mūrcchanās* of the Gāndhāra-grāma. (78)

*Ta-dha-ri-ga-ma-pa-ni-sa-ri*, *ri-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni-sa-ca*, *sa-ri-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni-ca*, *ni-sa-ri-ga-ma-pa-dha-ca*, *dha-ni-sa-ri-ga-ma-pa-ca*, *pa-dha-ni-sa-ri-ga-ma-ca*, *ma-pa-dha-ni-sa-ri-ga-ca*; these are the *mūrcchanās* of the Gāndhāra scale (*grāma*). Now, regarding the *mūrcchanās*: it is that wherein the notes (*svaras*) coalesce (*saṃmūrchanti*) and attain the state of a melody (*rāga*).
Bharatas call that "mūrcchanā," which arises from the *grāma*;
furthermore,
it is where the very resonant (*mūrcchita*) tone attains the state of *rāga*.
And having reached her, the sage spoke to her as she lay unconscious:
"Those [notes] arising from the scales (grāma), joined with the seven notes, shall be twenty-one in the three scales. (80)
*sarigamapadha-nī* are the *mūrcchanās* of the *ṣaḍja-grāma*;
*mapadhanisari-ga* are the *mūrcchanās* of the *madhyama-grāma*;
and *gamapadhanisa-ri* are the *mūrcchanās* of the *gāndhāra-grāma*. (81)
Now, their names are Lalitā, Gāndhārī, Citrā, Rohiṇī, Mataṅgajā,
Sauvīrā, Varṇamadhyā, Ṣaḍjamadhyā, and Pañcamī. (82)
Matsarī, Mṛdumadhyā, Śuddhāntā, Kalāvatī,
Tīvrā, Raudrī, Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Khecarī, Varā,
Nādavatī, and Viśālā are renowned throughout the three musical scales (grāmas).
"Twenty-one mūrcchanās have been declared by the Moon-crested Lord," [it was said].
As the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) played the mūrcchanā, a vast canopy of sounds from his flute spread forth;
the women of Raṅga were pierced by the floods of his arrows, just as the armies of the Lord of Rati (Kāma) are struck by the showers of his bodiless shafts.
He states this purpose:
"By performing *mūrcchanā* before Śiva, even a killer of a Brahmin is liberated.
Now, the *tālas*.

The *mūrcchanās* themselves would be the *tālas*, pure and based on the ascending scale. But Dāmodara says that those [elements] by which the applications (*prayoga*) are expanded, depending upon all the remaining *mūrcchanās*, [are the *tālas*]. 87.
There are likewise forty-nine tānas arising from the seven notes (svaras).
From those very [notes], other distinct kūṭatānas arise;
their divisions are so numerous that who could describe them in their entirety? ||88-89||
There are many subdivisions of *grāmas*, *mūrchanās*, and *tānas*;
however, they have not been described here because they are of no use for the present subject and are difficult to understand.
This has been stated in the section on *tānas*: [90]
These multiplied by five thousand become thirty-three thousand. Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the description of the *varṇa*: the tone (*svara*) employed at the commencement of the act of singing is called a *varṇa*.
It is of four kinds: stationary (sthāyin), ascending (ārohin), descending (avarohin), and passing (sañcārī).
He states the definition for each:
"If there is the repeated application of only a single note, it is stationary."
That [note] should be known as the *sthāyin* (stationary) tone; the other two are named according to their literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñaka*).

The "other two" are the ascending tone (*ārohisvara*) and the descending tone (*avarohisvara*), and they are so called because their names correspond to their meanings. The meaning is: it ascends, thus it is "ascending" (*ārohin*); it descends, thus it is "descending" (*avarohin*).
Through the blending of these, the tone is designated as *sañcārī* (moving).
The phonemes of these fixed, ascending, and descending notes become ornaments, especially through their arrangement.
And therein:
There are twenty-six *sthāyin* (stationary) notes, twelve *ārohin* (ascending),
twelve *sañcārin* (transitory), and twelve *avarohin* (descending).
Thus, the sixty-two well-known ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) have been proclaimed.
I have not proclaimed them here, as I have become weary of the prolixity of the texts.
He states the purpose of the ornaments:
"A firm appearance regarding the knowledge of the *svarajas* and the attainment of passion arise."
The purpose of the ornaments is the variety of vocal qualities (*varṇa*) and knowledge [of their application].
He speaks of the *grahasvara*: that which is applied at the beginning of a song and so forth is called the *grahasvara*. 98–99.
He describes the *aṃśasvara* (the partial tone): that which manifests the *rati* (emotional flavor) in song, to which all [other tones] conform,
and which itself attains the status of the *graha* through the application of the *nyāsa* and other [structural notes].
"He whose abundance exists everywhere—that vocal part is like a king" (100).

The author of the *Gītaprakāśa* states that the singer (*vādī*) is the one who determines the *rāgas* and so forth. By the phrase "who himself has attained the state of a *graha*," the meaning is that the *aṃśasvara* itself is the cause of the *grahasvara*.
For this very reason, in the *Māgha* [Kāvya]:
"Because he is not insignificant and because he is the preeminent one, like the primary note among the other musical tones,
rival kings become his attendants.
And furthermore:
Those which are said by the wise to be the life-force of the *rāgas* are called the *aṃśa-svaras*.
Thus he speaks of the *nyāsa-svara*:
that which brings the song and so forth to completion is declared to be the *nyāsa-svara*. (102–103)
He speaks of *jāti* (birth/style): that from which the birth of passion arises is *jāti* here; it is the mother of passion.
It is threefold: the pure (*śuddhā*), the modified (*vikṛtā*), and the mixed (*saṅkīrṇakā*), which arises from the union of the two. (104)
Furthermore, there are seven pure *jātis*, which are designated by the names of the notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*;
the remaining ones are those same [notes] modified through the mixture of modifications (*vikṛti*). ||105||
Thus, others say there are two types.
As it was stated by Harināyaka:
"Furthermore, the *jātis* are combined with both pure and modified [syllables]."
"Thus eighteen are designated as the mothers of the *rāgas*.
This very position appears to be the principal one, since it was accepted by the ancient masters. As it is stated in another treatise:
'The Ṣāḍjārṣabhī, Gāndhārī, Mādhyamī, and likewise the Pāñcamī...'"
And then there is Dhavala; these seven are the pure (śuddha) jāti scales:
Ṣaḍjakaiśika, Ṣaḍjamadhyamā, followed by Gāndhārapañcamī, Āndhrī, and likewise Ṣaḍjodīcyavatī. ||107-108||
Kārmāravī, Nandayantī, Gāndhārodīcyavā,
Madhyamodīcyavā, Raktagāndhārī, and Kaiśikī—
thus eleven modified (vikṛta) melodic scales have been proclaimed by Bharata and others.
Now we shall explain the pure, perfected, and modified causes of these [diseases]. ||110||
